title: Northrop’s robot space mechanic is a new way to keep satellites at work longer
teaser: Northrop's advanced robot spacecraft can now extend satellite life by attaching modular systems, signaling a major shift toward sustainable space repair.
summary: Northrop Grumman is pioneering 'in-orbit servicing' with its advanced Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), marking a shift toward sustainable space infrastructure. The MRV utilizes robotic arms and modular propulsion systems (MEPs) to extend the operational life of satellites, rather than waiting for them to fail from fuel depletion. For example, the Optus satellite, launched in 2009, could receive an estimated six years of service extension. Previously, MEVs have already provided such services. This new technology represents a significant leap, as the MRV is also designed to be refueled in orbit, demonstrating crucial capabilities needed for future large-scale space maintenance and upgrades.
author: Tim Fernholz
content: High above the Earth, a new generation of robots designed to keep satellites working longer is replacing its predecessor - quite literally. This week, a spacecraft built and operated by Northrop Grumman called a Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) unplugged from a communications satellite operated by the Australian firm Optus. For more than a year, the MEV spacecraft has been stuck to the back of the Optus satellite, keeping it in the right place in space so it can continue its mission. Now, the satellite life-extension spacecraft is leaving to make room for its replacement. In July, four new Northrop spacecraft launched into orbit on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. One is called the Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), a powerful satellite equipped with two advanced robotic arms that was developed by DARPA, the U.S. military research organization. The other three are called Mission Extension Pods, or MEPs, smaller, simpler satellites that are essentially modular propulsion systems. Those four spacecraft are currently headed for targets around 27,000 miles above the Earth. In 2027, the MRV will use its robotic arms to attach one of the MEP pods to the Optus satellite, which should keep it in orbit for years to come. The satellites that provide communications or scan the planet with various sensors only last for so long. They typically fail when they run out of fuel to stay in the right place, not because their computers and transceivers stop working. The Optus satellite was launched in 2009, and designed for a 15-year lifespan. If all goes well, the satellite could fly - and generate revenue - for another six years. Now, cheaper launch costs and lower-cost space components are making spacecraft repair missions a reality. The goal is "a paradigm shift where we can see space as sustainable, with a more resilient architecture and infrastructure base where we can do things like spacecraft repairs, life extension, or even upgrades and maintenance of satellites," according to Northrop's director of logistics and servicing, Cassie Wong. There are two MEVs in orbit right now, launched in 2019 and 2020, which have provided 10 years of life extension to three customers, including two different Intelsat spacecraft and the Optus satellite. MEV-1 will wait in a parking orbit for another customer, while MEV-2 is currently attached to its Intelsat customer until 2030. The Mission Robotic Vehicle, or MRV, represents an evolution of the business model. Satellite operators buy and own the MEPs, which are permanently attached to their spacecraft. That frees up the MRV to service more vehicles, creating a cheaper offering. The offering requires some serious technology chops. The vehicles need to autonomously approach one another and dock safely, not a simple task when both are moving at velocities of thousands of miles an hour. The MEVs use a docking probe to plug in and hang onto satellite thruster nozzles. Meanwhile, the MRVs will need to carefully attach the MEPs using their robotic arms. Unlike most satellites, the MRV is designed to be refueled in orbit - in part, a proof of concept for the kind of capabilities other satellites will need if this kind of in-orbit servicing becomes a norm. Right now, the extra cost and weight of such adaptations keeps spacecraft operators from investing in them. Indeed, the current trend in satellites is flying lots of cheap, effectively replaceable spacecraft in low orbits, as Starlink and Amazon LEO do. On the other hand, spacecraft keep getting bigger, and there are plenty of expensive, large satellites in orbit that could benefit from life extension. Wong hopes that the MRV will take on other missions in the future, adding new components to satellites as well as adjusting their orbits. That's likely to include defense customers, given the number of expensive satellites it owns in high orbits, and DARPA's involvement in developing the MRV's arms. Indeed, the U.S. Space Force has previously characterized a Chinese servicing spacecraft with robotic arms as a weapon, since it could theoretically grapple and degrade a rival satellite. Northrop says that its vehicles are focused on servicing missions. The vehicle could also be used in LEO, Wong says, to extend the life with valuable assets there. The startup Katalyst Space is attempting a similar mission to extend the life of a NASA space telescope after malfunctions left its vehicle tumbling last month. The company has a fix in place and hopes to complete the mission.

title: Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Neo4j GraphTalk event
teaser: Graph intelligence is transforming fraud detection, enabling systems to uncover hidden networks of bad actors by connecting otherwise invisible data points.
summary: Graph intelligence is critical for enterprises scaling AI, acting as a knowledge layer that gives Large Language Models (LLMs) context beyond their training data. This architecture, often called GraphRAG, ensures better accuracy and governance by externalizing organizational knowledge. Use cases demonstrate significant value: one POC identified over $100 million in tax fraud, while another in pharma used Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to spot complex, hidden anti-counterfeiting networks. These models combine rules-based logic with GNNs—exposing relationships that cannot be seen by isolated analysis or human intuition. The graph layer reveals connections between primary fraudsters and lower-volume participants, making detection more thorough and scalable.
author: Victoria Gayton
content: Graph intelligence is fast becoming the enterprise's missing connective tissue - the knowledge layer that lets models move from clever prototypes to reliable, decision‑grade systems. By preserving relationships across fragmented data, it gives artificial intelligence the context needed to produce more accurate answers and support informed action. At the Neo4j GraphTalk event , the conversation wasn't about another point product. It reflected a broader architectural shift in how enterprises connect data and supply context to AI systems at scale, according to theCUBE Research's John Furrier . "This is an event that brings all the industry insiders, technologies and customers together to talk about the innovations in AI at the graph level - really powering the secret sauce for what we're seeing scaling AI," he said. "That's ontologies; that's getting data fast, feeding the AI and having intelligence. It's becoming the key piece." During the Neo4j GraphTalk event and post-event coverage , Furrier spoke with Neo4j Inc. leaders, partners and customers in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE's livestreaming studio. Discussions centered on how knowledge graphs are grounding agent stacks at scale, how production use cases are demonstrating the value of connected data, and how partnerships are accelerating graph intelligence across platforms. (* Disclosure below.) Here are three key insights you may have missed from theCUBE's coverage of the Neo4j GraphTalk event: Insight #1: Graph intelligence grounds agents in an enterprise knowledge layer. As generative AI moves beyond experimentation, enterprises are converging on an architecture that grounds large language models in trustworthy organizational data. The enterprise knowledge layer keeps an organization's ontology, data and agent memory outside the model, allowing those assets to remain accessible and governed, according to Philip Rathle (pictured), chief technology officer of Neo4j Inc. "Enterprise knowledge layer is the big topic," he told theCUBE. " GraphRAG describes the pattern of having an LLM call out to a knowledge graph so that you externalize your knowledge in context. It doesn't live in the model. It lives in a system of knowledge. And that gives you better accuracy, explainability and governance." Independent research and a real-world proof point provide evidence for that architecture. The U.K.'s National Innovation Centre for Data found that GraphRAG made agents 80% more "truthful" than vector-only retrieval while enabling them to answer more than twice as many questions and use tokens more efficiently. In a recent engagement with a national tax agency, graph models delivered measurable value by exposing connections obscured in conventional tables, Rathle noted. "Forty-eight hours from the start of a POC, they identified more than $100 million in tax fraud," he said during GraphTalk. "If you generalize it, if you've been walking around limited with your blinders because you're looking at this data in 2D, you bring the data into a graph view and all of a sudden all these things become blindingly obvious, which before you just simply couldn't see." Here's theCUBE's complete video interview with Philip Rathle: Insight #2: Connected context exposes hidden risks and guides action. Graph intelligence exposes relationships that conventional tools and human analysts can miss. In Gilead Sciences Inc.'s pharmaceutical anti-counterfeiting work, a three-layer detection model combines rules-based logic for known patterns, traditional machine learning for statistical anomalies and graph neural networks for relationship-based fraud schemes , according to Thomas Luu , director of global product security at Gilead. "With the implementation of graph neural networks with Neo4j, we were able to really surface these hidden networks and enable us to analyze our data to a level and to a scale that was not possible before because of human limitations," Luu told theCUBE. "Fraud doesn't happen with just one transaction. It happens across a lot of entities, and a lot of these entities are hidden." Graph intelligence doesn't replace Gilead's existing fraud-detection methods; it adds a relationship layer that surfaces what rules and statistical anomalies can't, Luu noted. Clustering algorithms can automatically connect a primary fraud actor with lower-volume participants whose activity might otherwise remain hidden in aggregate data. "We don't want to just rely on one technique," Luu said during the event. "Rules are great, ML is great, but when you combine them with GNNs and the graph layer, that's when you start seeing things you never could before." Here's theCUBE's complete video interview with Thomas Luu: Connected context can also give AI agents a foundation for more autonomous security investigations. Icite Inc. normalizes customer identity data into a graph-based knowledge layer that agents can traverse to surface connections, establish behavioral baselines and identify deviations, according to Wes Mullins , founder and chief executive officer of Icite. "We can start autonomously going out and doing work for the security team," he told theCUBE. "That's really the goal. Let the agents handle the routine traversal so your analysts can focus on the decisions that actually require human judgment." Here's theCUBE's complete video interview with Wes Mullins: Insight #3: Graph intelligence makes enterprise context reusable and adaptive. A shared intelligence layer can provide a reusable foundation for agent development across large enterprise environments. In Microsoft Corp.'s supply-chain work, modeling a bill of materials as a graph allowed teams to preserve relationships and metadata rather than rebuilding that context for every agent, according to Jeevan Pathuri , vice president of software engineering at Microsoft. "We were able to build 10 to 15 agents in production in a matter of a few weeks," he said. "Without this kind of connected intelligence, we would have had to build these agents individually, one after the other, kind of rediscovering the relationships and the metadata along the way, versus having all of this created once and making it available for many scenarios." Here's theCUBE's complete video interview with Jeevan Pathuri: CommonThread AI Inc. applies a similar principle to go-to-market workflows, where disconnected tools fragment segmentation, ideal customer profiles, messaging and market data. A graph database gives teams a shared view of those relationships while allowing their broader business context to evolve with economic, political and market conditions, according to Tim Gosnell , chief executive officer of CommonThread AI. "The only way we can do that is by having a larger context window. Let's build that larger context window," Gosnell told theCUBE. "The more we build that larger context window, the more we understand what's going on across our business, and then we keep updating that. As things change, we keep getting new and adaptive context." title: AI nuclear power firm Fermi finally has a new CEO
teaser: Fermi appoints veteran executive Lee McIntire as new CEO to lead its AI nuclear power venture developing Project Matador in Amarillo, Texas.
summary: AI nuclear power firm Fermi has named Lee McIntire, a board member with experience at TerraPower and CH2M Hill, as its new CEO. This appointment comes after the company fired co-founder Toby Neugebauer months ago. Fermi America is developing Project Matador in Amarillo, Texas, which will use nuclear reactors to power data centers. The recent announcement, alongside securing TensorWave as a customer lease for this project, boosted the stock by nearly 23%. Chairman Marius Haas stated that Lee's 40 years of experience delivering large, complex projects make him ideal to lead Fermi in its construction and power delivery phase.
author: Kirsten Korosec
content: Fermi, the AI nuclear power firm, has named a new CEO more than three months after firing co-founder Toby Neugebauer from the top executive post. Fermi said Wednesday it has hired Lee McIntire, an independent member of the company's board who has held chief executive positions at CH2M Hill and TerraPower , the nuclear power startup founded by Bill Gates. Fermi America, which was co-founded by former U.S. Energy Secretary Rick Perry, is developing an AI campus in Amarillo, Texas, called Project Matador that will eventually use nuclear reactors to power data centers. The announcement, along with Monday's news that it had signed TensorWave as its first binding customer lease for its Project Matador campus, provided a welcome boost to Fermi's stock. (The stock is up nearly 23% since Monday.) The young company took a hit in April when Neugebauer and CFO Miles Everson were pushed out of the company. At the time, the company described the executive shakeup, along with other plans including a corporate headquarters in Dallas, as Fermi 2.0 . "Fermi's next chapter is a construction and power delivery story, and we believe Lee is the ideal executive to lead Fermi through that process," Marius Haas, Fermi's chairman of the board, said in a statement. "The job now is to build on schedule, on budget, and safely. Lee has spent 40 years delivering exactly this kind of large, complex project. He also knows Fermi from the inside, having served on our board through our latest period of growth, and he brings a reputation for integrity that Fermi's customers, employees, regulators, and neighbors can rely on."

title: Saber denies replacing Rideshare Stimulator’s writers with ChatGPT
teaser: A former writer claims Saber replaced her with ChatGPT on a new game; CEO denies the threat.
summary: A dispute has surfaced regarding generative AI's role in Saber Interactive’s 'Rideshare Stimulator.' Former lead writer Stella Sacco alleges she was replaced by ChatGPT during development, noting that passenger voices and written content appear to be AI-generated. CEO Matthew Karch countered this claim, stating that neither Saber nor Unigine have replaced any writers with AI, emphasizing the company's continued hiring of its 3000+ employees. While Karch admits that 'Rideshare Stimulator' incorporates AI—such as in an experimental infinite-passenger mode to enhance gameplay and NPC behavior—Sacco argues this usage fundamentally undermines his statement that human writing was key, arguing they are attempting to mislead about the extent of AI involvement.
author: Jay Peters
content: After a former lead writer claimed Saber "replaced me with ChatGPT," CEO Matthew Karch now claims, "Neither Saber nor Unigine have replaced any writers with AI," for the Rideshare "Stimulator" game announced last month, developed by Unigine. The writer, Stella Sacco, says differently, however, posting on Bluesky that "I was lead writer on this one! And Saber replaced me with ChatGPT midway through development. All the passenger voices were AI too. Either they changed direction at some point or they're not disclosing it on Steam." Saber describes Rideshare "Stimulator" as an "immersive driving simulation game that puts you behind the wheel as a rideshare business owner," and the segments shown in a teaser trailer appear to include AI-generated writing and audio for the simulated riders who are being picked up. The game's Steam listing does not currently include any disclosure about using generative AI. A statement from Karch provided to The Verge says, "The game will also feature an experimental, free-ride mode that by necessity incorporates AI as the number of passengers in the game is infinite. We are firm believers in using AI tools to improve or enhance gameplay experiences and improve NPC behavior as we have done since Saber was founded in 2001," it continued, also claiming that "As the industry has continued to contract, Saber continues to hire. None of our 3000+ employees have to worry about being replaced by AI." Sacco replied to Karch's statement in a message sent to The Verge . "My indignation at being called a liar by that statement aside, you can't meaningfully say both 'writers wrote the story' and 'computers wrote the text,'" Sacco says. "If rides I wrote are in there, and also rides AI wrote or will write are in there, then AI was still used, and I was still replaced, just as Saber told me they were doing in December 2023. They're trying to have it both ways. You can't win on the labor part of the statement while you admit you took work away from labor in the next part. It's ridiculous."

title: Nailed it: Toolstation gives its store IT an ASUS NUC refurb
teaser: Toolstation upgraded its outdated store tills with compact ASUS NUC mini-PCs to boost speed and security across 550+ UK branches.
summary: Retail giant Toolstation refreshed its entire technology estate, replacing old, slow Linux-based PoS terminals across more than 550 branches. The legacy systems struggled with aging hardware, lacking necessary security patches, and hindering rapid business growth. To modernize operations while maintaining a compact store layout, Toolstation adopted the ASUS NUC mini-PC (specifically NUC 13), running ChromeOS Flex. This shift allowed staff to utilize enhanced functionality at the counter—from stock checking to customer data pulls—without leaving the till. The transition integrates with a wider Google Workspace ecosystem and addresses industry needs for strong cybersecurity, ensuring reliability and uptime in key retail locations where online sales only account for a fraction of total spending.
content: When Toolstation's customers walk into a branch, work has usually paused somewhere else. A plumber, decorator or electrician is there because a plug won't fit, a roller has worn out, or the van needs restocking with brushed-steel double sockets. It is a place where trades and dedicated DIYers go when they need to get on with the job. Toolstation's point-of-sale terminals therefore need to keep pace with staff answering questions, checking stock and closing the sale before a quick visit turns into a long wait. "We know that we can provide top-quality, industry-leading customer service, but we need the IT functionality behind that to back us up," says Simon Marshall, store manager at Toolstation's Bridgwater branch. Founded in 2003, the retailer has grown to more than 550 UK branches stocking over 25,000 products for trade and DIY customers. The newer Toolstation GO format pushes the convenience model further, with smaller high-street locations, digital kiosks and local ranges shaped by store-level insight. That growth, online and in stores, has strained parts of the technology estate. Some in-store systems still ran on aging Linux-based hardware that had become slow, difficult to patch and awkward to support across a large branch network. At the Bridgwater store, close to head office, manager Simon Marshall says the old terminals were "very slow, very clunky". They had been fine for a smaller business, he says, but "due to our rapid growth, they quickly became unsuitable" for the role. The legacy PoS running on a custom Linux build was one instance of hardware no longer up to the task. "We had a struggle with our legacy equipment. We were unable to support the operating systems with security patches, which then became an operational inefficiency for our support teams. This then created security concerns, where we were unable to manage our antivirus and any other support around that which again, in turn, created an operational overhead," explains Corron Mlcak, IT end user technology lead, Toolstation. Toolstation concluded it needed to refresh the entire technology estate, from contact centers, warehouses and distribution hubs to its countrywide network of branches. The first decision was to build on the Google Chrome ecosystem already in use elsewhere in the business. The second was to find hardware that could run that model at the till without reintroducing the size, support and peripheral problems of the old estate. Retail wants better IT, but not more mess Retailers keep investing in technology even as store IT teams are asked to support more devices and software with limited local help. Gartner forecasts global enterprise IT spending in the retail market will grow 7.4 percent in 2026 to $233 billion. That spend reflects a shift in operational priorities: staff need reliable PoS systems with instant access to product and HR data, while head office wants tighter reporting and standardized processes. Security teams, meanwhile, are prioritizing device protection and patching, and finance is keen to avoid the ongoing expense of dispatching IT engineers to update individual branch devices by hand. Given that online sales still only account for a quarter to one-third of total UK retail spend, according to the ONS , stores remain a focal point for technology investment. A Business Research Insights report estimated that one-fifth of retail tech investment goes into improving in-store technology, while smart PoS accounts for over one-third of retail store tech deployments because integrated payment systems can speed up transactions and improve the customer experience. ASUS echoes this sentiment. "Retailers are trying to control IT overheads and support costs while modernizing aging infrastructure for newer software requirements," says Chris Davies, ASUS Country Product Manager for the NUC Mini PC Division. "At the same time, they need to strengthen cyber resilience and reduce hardware downtime, because both have a direct effect on costs and customer experience." The UK 2025/26 Cyber Security Breaches Survey found that 31 percent of retailers and wholesalers had experienced a breach or attack during the previous year. In the most extreme attacks, such as those experienced by M&S and Co-Op, breaches can cost hundreds of millions and significantly impact day-to-day operations such as getting stock into store and serving customers. Customer comes first "Customer service is at the core of our business model," explains Bridgwater branch manager Simon Marshall. "Customers do like to come in and out as quickly as possible... so having a system that keeps up with the speed of staff is integral to that." The old Linux systems were capping Toolstation's ambitions. The retailer wanted a counter terminal that could do more than open a cash drawer, process card payments, and print receipts: a device that could run web apps, check stock, pull customer information, support new sales processes and, increasingly, sit inside a managed cloud environment. "Retailers aren't really buying PCs, they're buying uptime," adds ASUS' Davies. "Every minute a till isn't working impacts customers, colleagues and revenue." Mini PC offers more from less "Being a retail environment, space is a premium, so we needed to make sure it could be tucked away, hidden away, so users didn't interfere with it while they were pulling stock out or doing their day-to-day business, but packed the punch that it needed," adds Mlcak. The ASUS NUC 13 is a mini-PC that fit the brief. It was compact enough to mount under the counter but still delivered the Intel-powered performance store workflows required. Mlcak says Toolstation was focused on performance after the legacy estate's slowness, and that the 13th Gen Intel Core i3 processor was its "optimal choice". He adds: "With the Intel chipset, it meant that we could be more optimal and we could expand our software choices. From that, we built upon a workstation environment as opposed to just a typical till environment." Marshall's store was one of the trial sites. "I was very impressed with the speed. As soon as I booted it up in the morning, it loaded straight away, no connectivity issues, everything fired up nice and quick." The newer software build also gave staff more functionality at the frontline tills, so that fewer tasks required leaving the counter for the manager's laptop. The size mattered too. "With the ASUS NUC 13 being much more compact than the old system, it saves a lot of space under the counter," Marshall says. That freed room for catalogs and other useful items, and cut the footprint occupied by a freestanding machine. A mini PC's compact form allows it to sit behind monitors, inside kiosks or under desks, which tidies cable runs and keeps hardware away from accidental knocks. ASUS claims the ASUS NUC form factor can cut idle power consumption by up to 50 percent compared with traditional desktops, and that a tool-free chassis simplifies replacement and upgrades. Market researchers expect demand for compact systems to continue growing. Global Market Insights valued the global mini PC market at $24.7 billion in 2025 and forecasts annual growth of 6.6 percent through 2035. The forecast covers a broader market than retail alone, but identifies commercial applications including kiosks, digital signage and other space-constrained systems as contributors to that growth. The operating system is part of the hardware decision Toolstation's rollout was more than a swap from one physical box to another. The ASUS NUC was configured to run ChromeOS Flex, fitting into a wider Google environment the retailer had already adopted: Google Workspace, Chromebooks in contact centers and ChromeOS tablets in warehouses, yards and on the road. Mlcak says Chrome Enterprise and enrollment tokens helped accelerate the rollout. Because the ASUS NUCs were certified and could be enrolled with enterprise licenses, Toolstation gained reporting, usage visibility, automated OS updates and patch management. "Without Chrome Enterprise and having the Enterprise enrollment tokens, I think that would have slowed us down dramatically," he says. ASUS argues the same pressure now defines much of the retail IT landscape. "IT teams are under pressure to support more stores with fewer resources. They need technology that's easy to deploy, simple to manage and reliable enough that they rarely have to think about it," says Davies. Toolstation's deployment of ASUS NUCs and other Chrome devices has produced a more consistent estate. Mlcak says: "By bringing all of the ecosystem into one place, it means that everything just works together with very minimal impact and/or support needed from any of my team." Support teams could write simpler guides, know what they were supporting and avoid maintaining a knowledge base spanning too many different operating systems. That matters because store staff are not IT technicians and should not have to be running Device Manager to update faulty drivers. Rolling out without closing the counter Toolstation avoided a big-bang change in stores. The team replaced thousands of units in phases, taking one device off, swapping it, checking it worked, then moving to the next. Mlcak says the team continued that model with "a bit of hyper-care behind it". Marshall says the Bridgwater store carried on trading while the work happened. "It didn't affect the store operation at all in a negative way," he says. The team changed part of the till estate, came back to change the rest, and kept the old system running until the new one was ready. The wider deployment ran in phases across the UK store estate alongside refreshes and infrastructure upgrades. ASUS says the return rate during the rollout was below 0.5 percent, against an industry average of three percent for a similar deployment. With the new environment fully operational, Mlcak says the IT team has seen "a significant drop" in support tickets around the devices, especially break-fix. "The overall concern about [till] slowness has definitely vanished," he says. "We don't have any tickets that are coming in around slowness anymore." He credits an 80-90 percent operational efficiency gain largely to the ASUS NUC deployment, spanning reduced downtime, low return rates, faster replacement, less support effort and better operational availability. Branch manager Marshall says staff now have confidence that when they approach the till, "it's going to work first time for them." Building out the branch Toolstation used ASUS NUCs as its store PoS endpoints, but retailers planning a broader branch refresh should also consider the display and network around the computer. ASUS groups those elements into a commercial portfolio of ASUS NUC mini PCs, monitors, and ExpertWiFi networking products, giving IT teams a common supplier for the principal components of the branch setup. This can result in simpler procurement, deployment, integration and operations. At the counter, an ASUS NUC can be mounted under a desk or using a suitable VESA mount. A conventional business monitor may suit a staff workstation, while a touchscreen can support a kiosk or assisted-service point. ProArt displays address design, signage, and catalog work where color accuracy is required. Compatible ASUS NUCs and monitors also support ASUS Power Sync over HDMI CEC, allowing staff to control both devices from the monitor when the computer is mounted out of reach. ExpertWiFi provides the network connecting those endpoints. The EBM68 can create up to five SSIDs, with VLANs used to separate PoS, staff, guest, IoT, and VPN traffic. It also supports backup internet connections and centralized administration through the ExpertWiFi app. ASUS's proposition therefore covers the compute running retail applications, the display used by staff or customers, and the network connecting them, with a more consistent procurement, deployment, warranty, and support model across sites. De-fragging the IT estate Refreshing the PoS with mini PCs was the headline part of the project, but Toolstation was also trying to make its wider IT estate less fragmented. It worked with ASUS and Google on a "grand design" across branches, distribution centers and contact centers, following the adoption of Google Chrome during COVID. The aim was not uniformity for its own sake, but a smaller ecosystem of hardware and software combinations to maintain. For stores, the ASUS NUCs running ChromeOS Flex became the PoS endpoint. Elsewhere in the business, ASUS Chromebook Plus devices and Chrome tablets extended the same Google-centered model to managers, contact center staff, warehouse teams and drivers. The point was not to make every device identical, but to reduce the number of hardware and software combinations Toolstation had to support. "The biggest benefit of having the ASUS devices and the Google ecosystem means that it's coherent across the organization," says Mlcak. "Previously, we had a lot of tech debt, and we supported many different operating systems." The unified environment has cut the range of hardware and software combinations Toolstation supports. It has also given the retailer a simpler model for procurement, deployment, installation, warranty and support. Toolstation's business is built around giving customers the right tool quickly, and its store IT refresh followed the same principle by getting the right technology tools into people's hands. Sponsored by ASUS.

title: Google’s Quick Share adds a tap-to-share mode
teaser: Google updated Quick Share for a tap-to-share mode, letting Android users easily exchange contacts, photos, and videos like Apple's AirDrop.
summary: Google is enhancing its Quick Share feature with a tap-to-share mode, making file exchange between Android devices easier. The update allows users to instantly send contacts, photos, and videos by bringing compatible phones close together for an 'instant, two-way exchange.' This functionality aims to better align the Pixel lineup with Apple's AirDrop and NameDrop features. Starting Wednesday, the update rolls out on Pixel 6 and newer devices and will soon be supported on forthcoming Samsung Galaxy models.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Alongside its Pixel 11 product launches on Wednesday, Google announced it is making fast sharing between its devices easier, with an improved version of Google's Quick Share feature (similar to Apple's AirDrop), rolling out now. The feature will now allow Android users to send their contact information, photos, videos, and more with a tap. To use the new version of Quick Share, you'll bring your Android device close to another compatible Android device for what Google calls an "instant, two-way exchange." Plus, you'll be able to share photos or videos from the phone's Share Sheet, then tap devices together to make the exchange. The addition brings the Pixel lineup more on par with the iPhone, as it follows the launch of the NFC-powered NameDrop feature in Apple's iOS 17, which similarly allowed iPhone users to share contacts, photos, or videos by touching phones. The Quick Share update is rolling out starting on Wednesday on Pixel 6 and newer devices, and will soon arrive on the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Fold8, and Flip8 as well. More devices will be supported by year-end, Google says.

title: Mesh, Automattic’s CRM for everyone, comes to Android
teaser: Automattic's CRM, Mesh, arrives on Android! Expect advanced AI features like asking 'who knows X company?' while keeping your data private.
summary:
Automattic's CRM, Mesh (formerly Clay), has launched on Android devices, significantly enhancing its accessibility and functionality. Users can now track professional and personal networks and manage contacts via features optimized for Android, including widgets and split-screen support. Looking ahead, the platform plans deep integration with Automattic’s messaging app, Beeper, which connects users across platforms like WhatsApp and X.
Mesh is also rolling out 'Nexus AI,' an AI feature that allows users to ask complex questions about their network—such as identifying contacts at a specific company or with certain expertise. Importantly, Mesh emphasizes privacy by ensuring stored data is not used for ad targeting. While currently favored by business users (70% of customers), the tool aims to serve both professional and individual consumers.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Mesh , the relationship manager and personal CRM acquired by WordPress.com's parent company, Automattic , last year, is now available to users on Android devices. The software allows users to privately visualize and keep track of the people in their personal and professional networks, add notes to people's contact information, and be reminded when to reach out. On Android , the company customized Mesh's app to work with key platform features, like split-screen and pop-up views. This allows users to access Mesh while working in other apps, like messages or email. It also supports keyboard shortcuts for foldables and tablets, in-app search, home screen widgets (with Material You colors that match your Android's wallpaper), and real-time sync across devices. Image Credits: Mesh The company's broader plans for Mesh could eventually see it tied more closely to Automattic's all-in-one messaging app, Beeper , which offers a way to connect with people across platforms, including through WhatsApp, Instagram, Signal, Messenger, X, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, Google Messages, and more. Already, Mesh and Beeper interoperate to some extent, as Mesh users can draft a text to someone in Beeper or click deep links in the app to visit a Mesh user's profile. In time, the company wants to add additional AI features that will make users of both products more productive in terms of managing their personal relationships. "We're thinking a lot about how can AI help you be a better friend and have better work and personal relationships?," Mesh co-founder Zachary Hamed told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this spring. "We have users who have ten-, twenty-, or fifty-thousand connections across multiple social media apps, across their work products. It's an impossible task to think and be conscientious with you, with each of those people, by yourself," he noted. Image Credits: Mesh Today, Mesh's Nexus AI is in early access, offering a way to use AI to navigate your network. That means users can ask questions like who they know at a particular company or who lives in a certain city, or who has expertise in a particular topic. The company is also experimenting with using AI technology to provide a voice-based, hands-free experience and an improved business card scanning feature. Importantly, personal information stored in Mesh isn't shared or used for ad targeting, the company says, as the product is supported by subscriptions . (It's free for up to 1,000 contacts, then has higher tiers for unlimited contacts and other features.) In time, Mesh may consider a bundled subscription with Beeper or other Automattic products, but has nothing to announce on that front at this time. Currently, the majority of Mesh's customers, or around 70%, are using the app for some type of business purpose. Mesh co-founder Matthew Achariam says Mesh's sweet spot is executives running bigger teams or those who have a tight network to stay in touch with. However, the company still thinks about the consumer use case, he notes. "The beauty of [serving business users] is that the same things they're using apply to every individual consumer. So every feature that we think about has to apply to both," he says. Mesh ( formerly Clay ) for Android will roll out to Google Play for phones, tablets, and foldables as a free download with in-app purchases.

title: AI-Backed Securities

title: The next big indie game publisher is taking some exciting swings
teaser: A new indie game puts you in the shoes of Diana, whose visions of the future are so potent they change reality just by being remembered.
summary: A new indie game concept features players assuming the role of Diana, whose life changes after an experimental implant grants her premonitions. Players must explore these visions of the future and commit key details to her memory in the present day. However, this power comes with significant consequences: every time a detail is committed, the very nature of the predicted future alters itself. This dynamic premise suggests complex narrative choices and high stakes for players.
author: Jay Peters
content: Players take on the role of Diana, a woman who discovers she can receive visions of the future after an experimental implant is embedded into her brain. Players will be tasked with exploring these visions of the future, focusing on specific moments and committing them to Diana's memory in the present day. Prescience comes with consequences, however, and as soon as Diana commits a detail to memory, the very future ahead of her changes.

title: Cats and dogs are missing meals after a popular smart feeder went down
teaser: A smart feeder outage has caused chaos for pet owners, with some pets reportedly missing crucial scheduled meals due to tech failures.
summary: An outage impacting Petlibro's smart pet ecosystem is preventing the scheduled operation of various connected devices. The problem, which began on Tuesday, has left some pets without meals because key feeding schedules are failing. While Petlibro initially assured users that local device settings would continue to function, many report missing dispensed food from specific units like RFID and Granary feeders. author: Emma Roth
content: A Petlibro outage is preventing its smart pet feeders and other devices from performing scheduled tasks, like dispensing food. The outage began on Tuesday, with users across Reddit reporting that their smart feeders, litter boxes, and water fountains have gone offline . Though Petlibro maintains that "existing settings and schedules stored locally on your device will continue to operate as programmed," many users say that's not the case. title: We don't serve pies, but we do like a Pi
teaser: A London pub's tipping machine was found running on a Raspberry Pi, showing how micro-computers are embedding themselves in daily commerce.
summary:
A humorous report observed a Raspberry Pi—a small single-board computer—integrated into a modern tipping machine at a London pub. This new technology helps streamline the process of leaving tips by allowing customers to tap their payment cards directly, bypassing older methods like physical coins or cash gestures.
While the device, identified as TiPJAR hardware, aims to 'relieve operational pain-point,' its presence highlights the increasing integration of complex tech into routine commercial life. The author suggests that while technology is useful for transactions, it should not replace proper staffing and wages.
content: offbeat We don't serve pies, but we do like a Pi What would be your tip for this stricken device? BORK!BORK!BORK! There is an old IT truism that the best tip anybody can give is "turn it off and turn it on again." But this is probably not the sort of tip that the staff at this London pub were expecting. Today's entry into the world of embedded borks comes from the tipping machine in a London pub, spotted by an eagle-eyed Register reader. Tipping culture has yet to take root in the UK to the same extent as in the US, but it is spreading. Rather than dropping a few coins into a jar or muttering "and one for yourself" while trusting that the employee behind the bar won't opt for a pint of Champagne, customers can tap a payment card on the machine to reward good service discreetly. "The pub didn't serve pies," our reader noted, "but it did have a Raspbian GNU/Linux screen on the bar logged in as 'pi.'" The bork fairy appears to have paid a visit and left the device's undercrackers on show. A Raspberry Pi is undeniably running behind the scenes, complete with an automatic login as "pi" and the wonderfully generic hostname "raspberrypi." Doubtless the password has been secured. The device itself appears to be an example of TiPJAR hardware , modestly described as a "ground-breaking system" that "relieves the operational pain-point of tipping and empowers staff to control tips." It has certainly delivered on the "breaking" part, since the only tip staff will be collecting is from wags commenting "have you tried turning it off and on again?" Oh, how they'll laugh. We were also delighted to see rc.local on the screen, surely a reference to one's local hostelry rather than some tedious startup script. The wonders of technology will never cease. Assuming they can boot past a terminal prompt. While we're sure an IT professional with a keyboard to hand could restore the device, doubtless asking only for a free beverage in return, we actually quite like these machines, so long as they don't end up being used by employers as a replacement for paying staff a suitable salary. It's certainly an improvement on scribbling on a credit card receipt, fumbling for non-existent change, or avoiding making awkward eye contact. ®
